title: Partial projected ensembles reveal slow tilt-constrained information spreading
authors: Yi-Rui Zhang, Yu-Jun Zhao, Han-Ze Li, Jian-Xin Zhong
abstract: Projected ensembles reveal information about quantum many-body dynamics beyond the reduced density matrix. Here we investigate how spatial constraints affect the emergence of this information in a kicked Ising chain with a spatially varying longitudinal field. We consider partial projected ensembles, obtained by measuring a remote region while leaving an intervening buffer unobserved. Our numerical results reveal a pronounced contrast between nearly ballistic correlation onset in the ergodic regime and strongly delayed onset in the tilt-constrained regime, corroborated by quantum mutual information. Despite these different onset scales, the conditional-state fluctuations decrease approximately exponentially with buffer length in both regimes. Full projected ensembles additionally exhibit slow relaxation and persistent measurement-basis dependence in their higher moments. We establish an information-theoretic characterization of the connected second moment and use a solvable dephasing model with effective-basis measurements to illustrate the separation of phase accumulation and coherence loss. Within this model, a factorially suppressed coupling envelope yields sublogarithmic spreading consistent with the finite-distance onset trends. Our results identify partial projected ensembles as probes of the distinction between the time required for correlations to develop and the information that remains accessible under partial observation.
summary: This paper analyzes quantum information spreading in a kicked Ising chain by using partial projected ensembles (PPEs). It finds that spatial constraints cause a dramatic difference in how fast correlations build up between ergodic and tilt-constrained regimes. The research provides an information-theoretic tool to distinguish between the physical time needed for correlations to develop and the information that can actually be measured when parts of the system are unobserved.
main_problem: The paper investigates how spatial constraints affect the emergence of quantum information about many-body dynamics, specifically comparing the time required for correlations to develop versus the information accessible under partial observation.
main_result: Partial projected ensembles reveal a strong contrast in correlation onset times between ergodic and tilt-constrained regimes, with the latter showing a significantly delayed buildup. The study establishes that partial observation probes the distinction between correlation development time and accessible information.
method: The authors use numerical simulations on a kicked Ising chain, employing partial projected ensembles (PPEs) and analyzing various information-theoretic diagnostics like quantum mutual information and moment distances.
model_or_system: The system is a kicked Ising chain subjected to a spatially varying longitudinal field, governed by a Floquet evolution operator. The analysis involves partitioning the chain into three regions: a target region (A), an unobserved buffer (E), and a measured region (B).
key_observables: Conditional-state fluctuations, quantum mutual information, connected second moment, and the onset time ($t^*$) for correlation buildup.
important_parameters: The control parameter $\Gamma$ (related to kick strength and Stark tilt), buffer length ($L_E$), and the comparison between the ergodic and tilt-constrained regimes.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the mathematical framework of projected ensembles and assumes the applicability of specific information-theoretic bounds ($\Delta \le \chi \le I_q$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the comparison of correlation onset times ($t^*$) in ergodic vs. Stark-constrained regimes, the decay of moment distances ($\Delta(k)$) with buffer length, and the evolution of mutual information ($I$) over time.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the concept of PPEs to probe information beyond the reduced density matrix. It analyzes the dynamics in two distinct regimes (ergodic vs. tilt-constrained), deriving quantitative scaling laws for the onset of correlations and demonstrating the separation of phase accumulation and coherence loss using a solvable dephasing model.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses non-equilibrium dynamics and information scrambling in systems exhibiting localization or strong disorder, which are central topics in condensed matter theory, particularly concerning Many-Body Localization (MBL) physics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Partial observation and proposed spreading laws. (a) Evolution in a Stark field with control parameter F and curvature β, followed by measurement of B and tracing out the buffer E, produces conditional states on A. Bloch spheres illustrate their distributions. (b),(c) Ballistic, logarithmic, and proposed sublogarithmic spreading correspond to linear, exponential, and factorial-type onset times versus buffer length LE.

FIG. 2. Regime diagnostics. (a) Half-chain von Neumann entropy, averaged over all Floquet eigenstates and divided by L, versus control parameter F. Inset: rescaling with Fc = 0.651 and ν = 0.84. (b1),(b2) Normalized circular quasienergy- spacing distributions for L = 12 at F = 0.2 and 0.8; dashed curves show circular-orthogonal-ensemble (COE) and Poisson benchmarks. Entropies use natural logarithms.

FIG. 3. Full projected ensembles at F = 0.8, averaged over 1000 random product states; t counts Floquet periods. (a),(b) Second- and third-moment trace distances ∆(k) to the initial- state-specific Scrooge reference, with LA = 2 and X-basis measurements. (c),(d) Residual second-moment distances versus L and measurement angle α for LA = 1,2; insets show first moments. Here α = π/2 is the X basis. Residuals and horizontal dashed lines use the last 200 saved times; inset lines in (a),(b) and dashed curves in (c),(d) are exponential fits.

FIG. 4. PPE connected second-moment trace distance ∆ for LA = 1, LB = 6, L = LE + 7, and X-basis measurement of B, averaged over 1000 random product states. (a),(c) F = 0.2; (b),(d) F = 0.8. Heatmaps show ∆(t,LE); crosses mark the 10−5 onset threshold and red dashed curves are the displayed fits. The light-cone labels distinguish the two sides of this threshold. Insets in (c),(d) show residuals at t = 20 and averaged over the last 200 saved times, respectively, with exponential fits. Time is in Floquet periods.

FIG. 5. Premeasurement quantum mutual information I = SA +SB −SAB, using natural logarithms, with LA = 1, LB = 6, and L = LE + 7. Results average 1000 random product states; t counts Floquet periods. (a),(c) F = 0.2; (b),(d) F = 0.8. Crosses mark I = 10−5 and red dashed curves are onset fits. Insets show I(t = 20) in (c) and the mean over the last 20 saved times in (d), with exponential fits. The 0.67 fit uses LE = 6–9; the 0.51 fit uses LE = 3–9 and describes a finite-time average.
